NSW TrainLink runs rail and coach services from Sydney to Bathurst. In town, the circuit sits on the south-western edge, close enough to the centre that many visitors walk or use event shuttles.
October here is spring at altitude, and the weather is not reliably mild. Campers usually pack for both ends of it:

- warm sleeping gear and layers for cold nights on the hill
- a waterproof jacket, because rain can sweep across the top
- a hat and sunscreen for long days on open grass
- earplugs, for sleeping while the engines run
Camping spots are ticketed and come with their own conduct rules.
The Mountain has a culture of its own.

**Accommodation goes early.** Bathurst town accommodation and on-circuit camping are both in high demand, and fans who return every year often rebook straight after the race. Orange and Lithgow are the usual fallbacks when both are full.

**Event rules apply.** Glass, alcohol limits, campfires and vehicle access in the camping areas are all controlled by event conditions. Organisers have tightened the rules on the Mountain over the years. Fans who ignore them risk having their gear confiscated or being removed.
**Merch and sides.** Team colours are everywhere: shirts, flags and camp-site banners. Rivalries are loud but mostly good-natured, and talking cars with the camp next door is part of the weekend.

**Cards, with cash as backup.** Most food and merchandise outlets at the circuit take cards and phone payments. Mobile networks can struggle under race-day crowds, though, so a little cash is a common fallback.

**The finish.** A 1000-kilometre race often comes down to the final stint. Leaving early to beat the traffic is how people miss the result. Exit queues on the Sunday evening are long whatever time people go.

Outside race weekends, Mount Panorama is a normal public road, Mountain Straight and Conrod Straight included. Anyone can drive a full lap in their own car. A strict 60 km/h limit applies, police enforce it, and drivers share the road with residents and other visitors.

Driving it in ordinary traffic shows how steep the climb to Skyline is, and how blind the drop into The Esses is. The National Motor Racing Museum sits beside the circuit at Murray's Corner, with race cars and Bathurst memorabilia, so it pairs naturally with a lap.

In town, the wide streets and nineteenth-century gold-rush buildings around Kings Parade are worth an afternoon. They make Bathurst feel like more than a racetrack, and the town is a short walk from the Mountain.

BIFF's 31st year runs October 6-15, 2026, a ten-day run that anchors Busan's autumn calendar. Expect a packed slate of films from dozens of countries, spanning new Asian cinema, world premieres and restored classics. This year's festival honors Michelle Yeoh as Asian Filmmaker of the Year, a slot that usually brings a retrospective screening and a public conversation. BIFF has always used the festival to spotlight Asian cinema first, Hollywood a distant second, so the crowd skews toward serious festival-goers and industry buyers over casual tourists.

Almost everything funnels through the Busan Cinema Center in Centum City, Haeundae-gu. The building itself is worth the trip regardless of programming: a vast cantilevered roof designed by Austrian firm Coop Himmelb(l)au, with an open-air theater underneath used for the opening and closing ceremonies. Take Busan Metro Line 2 to Centum City Station and follow exit signs toward the Busan Cinema Center; it's a short walk from the station, next to the BEXCO convention center and Shinsegae Centum City department store.

Screenings during the festival also spread to satellite cinemas nearby, including CGV and Lotte Cinema branches in Centum City and Haeundae, so check your ticket for the exact theater, not just "BIFF."

Ticketing for BIFF opens online before the festival and typically sells out popular gala and red-carpet screenings within minutes. Standard rules to expect, though you should confirm each on the official site:

- Tickets are sold per screening, not as a festival pass, through the official BIFF website and app.
- A festival badge or online account registration is usually required before you can buy.
- Popular titles and any Michelle Yeoh-related events will move fastest; have your preferred screening times ready before the sale window opens.
- Same-day or standby tickets sometimes appear at the venue box office for less in-demand slots.
Confirm timing and tickets on the official BIFF site, since sale dates, prices and screening venues shift year to year.

Arrive at least 20-30 minutes before any screening; BIFF enforces seating by ticket time, and latecomers are often held until a break in the film. Q&A sessions with directors or cast frequently follow gala screenings, so don't sprint for the exit the moment credits roll. Most signage and subtitles run in Korean and English, and staff at the Busan Cinema Center's info desk switch easily between both.

For meals between screenings, the surrounding Centum City strip has fast, affordable options built for exactly this rhythm: quick Korean and Japanese chains rather than long sit-down restaurants. If you're catching multiple films across venues, budget the walk or a short taxi ride, since satellite cinemas aren't always adjacent to the Cinema Center itself.

removed: Thiru Vi Ka Park sits on Thuru Vi Ka Park Road in Shenoy Nagar, a residential pocket of central Chennai. It's a walled, gated green space built around a walking track, not a garden of monuments or ruins. Locals use it as a fitness loop: joggers, walkers, and older residents doing morning stretches on the grass verges. The pond and landscaped beds inside make it a step up from a bare municipal ground, which is why it holds a strong 4.5 rating across over 2,000 reviews.

Getting there is straightforward by autorickshaw or taxi to Shenoy Nagar; the park address (No 13, Thuru Vi Ka Park Road) is well known to local drivers. Shenoy Nagar Metro station, on the Chennai Metro Blue Line, is the nearest rail link, putting you within a short auto ride of the gate. Pair a morning visit here with breakfast at one of the small idli-and-filter-coffee stalls that dot the surrounding residential streets, a low-key way to see how the neighbourhood actually runs its day.

Most of the world's book business meets here. Rick Steves calls it a "huge book fair and publishers' convention", and both halves of that are accurate. The 2026 edition runs **Wednesday 7 to Sunday 11 October**.

Publishers, literary agents, translators and rights scouts fill the halls on the weekdays. They sit at small tables in back-to-back meetings, buying and selling translation and film rights. On Saturday and Sunday the halls fill with readers, students, school groups and costumed cosplayers.
The fair fills the **Messe Frankfurt** exhibition grounds, between the city centre and Bockenheim. Public transport beats driving here.

- **S-Bahn:** lines S3, S4, S5 and S6 to *Frankfurt (Main) Messe*.
- **U-Bahn:** U4 to *Festhalle/Messe*, close to the City entrance by the Festhalle.
- **From the airport:** take the S-Bahn into the city and change if needed. Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof is one stop from Messe on the S-Bahn.
- **On foot:** the Hauptbahnhof is a straightforward walk away if the trains are packed.
Hotels across Frankfurt and as far out as Mainz, Darmstadt and Wiesbaden fill up during fair week, and prices go up. Book early, or stay in a neighbouring city on a direct train line.
The grounds are big. Covered moving walkways (the *Via Mobile*) connect the halls, and getting from one end to the other still takes time. Plan around a few halls, not the whole site.

- **Check the online hall plan first.** Exhibitor locations change every year.
- **Use the cloakrooms.** Bags fill up fast with catalogues and free proofs.
- **Find the Agora.** This open-air square between the halls has food stands, outdoor stages and seating.
- **Look for the Guest of Honour pavilion.** It usually has the most designed space on the grounds.

On the final Sunday, the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade (*Friedenspreis des Deutschen Buchhandels*) is presented in the Paulskirche in the old town. The ceremony is broadcast, and it marks the end of fair week for much of the city.

On trade days, everything runs on appointments. Agents and rights staff book meetings in tight half-hour slots weeks in advance. Their stand tables are not for walk-up pitches. If you are an author looking for representation, the fair is the wrong place to approach agents unannounced. Send queries by email beforehand.

On public days, the rules relax. Stands sell books, publishers run signings, and author talks fill the stages. Popular signings build queues well before they start, so check the event programme on the official app or website and get there early.

- Your ticket type sets which days you can enter. Trade and public tickets are not the same.
- Buy online and bring the digital ticket. Box office queues at the entrances are slow on Saturday morning.
- Many visitors get to Saturday and Sunday in costume. The cosplay crowd is a regular part of the weekend.
- Carry water and a snack. Food lines in the halls get long at lunchtime.
Confirm timing, ticket categories and entry rules on the official Frankfurter Buchmesse site before you travel.

[FAQ 3] Q: Which station should I use to reach the parade? A: For the start near the Imperial Palace, use Marutamachi or Imadegawa station on the Karasuma subway line. For the finish at Heian Shrine, use Higashiyama or Jingu-Marutamachi station on the Tozai line.

Kyoto stages three great festivals a year, and Jidai Matsuri is the one that turns the streets into a walking history textbook. On October 22, 2026, roughly two thousand people in costume move from the old Imperial Palace grounds down through the city to Heian Shrine, each block of marchers representing a different era of Japanese history, in reverse chronological order from the Meiji Restoration back to the eighth century.

That structure is what makes it different from a generic parade. You are not watching a themed float show; you are watching Kyoto's own idea of its history, staged by neighbourhood associations that have done this since 1895.

Two portable shrines (mikoshi) carrying the spirits of Emperors Kanmu and Komei, Kyoto's founding and final emperors, close out the religious core of the event. Costumes, armor, and hairstyles are researched and rebuilt by local textile and craft guilds, not rented from a costume house, which is why Kyoto treats this parade as a living archive as much as a spectacle.
Most spectators pick one fixed spot along the route rather than following the parade, since it moves at walking pace over several hours and side streets fill in fast once it passes.
Standing room along most of the route costs nothing. You simply find a curb along Karasuma-dori, Oike-dori, or Kawaramachi-dori and wait.

Paid reserved seating, arranged through the Kyoto City Tourism Association, is sold for sections nearer the start of the route, usually as grandstand-style seats with a clear sightline. This is worth it if you want to sit rather than stand for a couple of hours, or if you are visiting with people who tire easily on their feet.
Confirm timing and tickets on the official site, since reserved-seat details and exact start times are set by the organizers each year and should not be assumed from a previous year's schedule.

Before the main parade even starts, there is a smaller, quieter ceremony worth knowing about: the Kurumayose, where the imperial mikoshi are formally sent off from the Kyoto Gyoen grounds with Shinto rites. It draws a much thinner crowd than the parade route itself, largely local families and shrine parishioners, and gives you a close, unhurried look at priests and shrine staff before the costumed procession takes over the streets. If you arrive early, this is the moment that rewards patience.

Late October in Kyoto sits between the last of the autumn heat and the start of proper cool weather, so mornings can be mild and afternoons can turn breezy once the sun drops behind the hills. The parade itself runs for several hours from late morning into early afternoon, but you do not need to watch the whole thing from one spot.

Most visitors budget one to two hours: enough to see a meaningful cross-section of eras pass, take photographs, and step away before the crowd context. Hundreds of thinner side ropes branch off the main rope like ribs. Those are what you actually hold. The two halves face each other across the Kumoji intersection, one team for the East and one for the West, and tens of thousands of people pack in on both sides.
